chapter_title: Interacting with Contracts in a React Frontend (Basic Setup)

screens.title: Interacting with Contracts in a React Frontend
screens.subtitle: Basic setup for connecting Web3.js, reading state, and sending transactions from a dApp

narration.text: In this lesson we'll move smart contract interaction from the command line into an interactive browser experience. You will learn how a React application talks to an injected Ethereum provider like MetaMask, how to create a Web3. js contract instance, and how to wire read and write operations into React state. This matters because end users expect immediate feedback and secure signing prompts from their wallet. For example, a simple Counter DApp displays a numeric state read from a contract and lets the connected user send a transaction to increment it via MetaMask. We'll also cover important safety checks: explicitly requesting accounts, estimating gas, and listening for account or network changes so the UI never shows stale data. By the end you should be able to initialize Web3 in a component, fetch view data for display, trigger a transaction and handle the wallet events that keep your UI accurate and secure. Consider: what will your app do differently if the user switches accounts while viewing a balance?

keyIdea.title: Core chapter idea
keyIdea.text: Use Web3.givenProvider or window.ethereum inside React to create a web3 instance, instantiate a contract with its ABI and address, and manage provider, accounts, and contract state with React Hooks to produce an interactive dApp experience.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will connect a React app to an injected Ethereum provider, manage Web3-related state with React Hooks, and perform both read and write operations against a deployed contract. First, you'll learn to detect the provider and request account access, which is essential so the wallet can sign transactions on behalf of the user. Second, you'll use useState and useEffect to hold the web3 instance, the connected accounts, and the contract instance so UI updates are consistent and predictable. Third, you'll call view functions like getCount to display contract state without requiring a transaction. Fourth, you'll implement UI controls that trigger state-changing functions like increment and handle asynchronous gas estimation and confirmations. Each objective ties directly to the Counter DApp example, teaching both the A P I calls and the UX patterns that make a dApp practical and safe.

screens.title: Why use React for dApps
screens.subtitle: Component structure and UI quality for on-chain interactions

narration.text: React is a practical choice for dApps because its component model maps naturally to the small, interactive pieces of a blockchain UI: wallet connection status, account info, contract state displays, and action controls that trigger transactions. A React component can initialize Web3 once, store the resulting objects in state, and re-render only when values change, which helps minimize unnecessary network calls. For example, a Counter component holds web3, accounts, contract, and count as state. When a user confirms an increment transaction, the contract state changes on-chain; React lets you fetch the updated value and re-render the display immediately. A common misconception is that Web3 complexity must live in backend services; while server-side scripting has its place, keeping user signing in the browser via an injected wallet is both more secure and more user-friendly. The key takeaway is to design small, testable components: one handles connection and provider detection, another fetches and displays contract data, and a third offers transaction controls. Thinking in components keeps your dApp modular, easier to debug, and responsive to wallet events. Why use React for dApps means component-based rendering together with hooks provides a predictable lifecycle for web3 initialization, state updates, and user-driven transactions.. In practical terms, component structure and ui quality for on-chain interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: React fits dApps
keyIdea.text: Component-based rendering together with hooks provides a predictable lifecycle for Web3 initialization, state updates, and user-driven transactions.

content.html:
Core Concept Why React for dApps
Definition & benefits
  • Components encapsulate wallet connection, contract reads, and transaction controls.
  • React re-renders only when state changes, keeping network calls predictable.
  • Hooks let you run side effects like initial Web3 setup and event subscriptions on mount.
Concrete example
A Counter component uses useState for web3, accounts, contract, and count. initWeb3 runs on mount to populate these values and fetch the count to display.
Misconception: "I'll store private keys in the UI for convenience." Never do that. Use injected wallets for signing.
Design pattern
Split responsibilities across components so connection logic, data fetching, and UI actions remain isolated. This reduces bugs when accounts or networks change.
Key takeaway
Design small components: connector, data reader, action controls. Keep signing in the user's wallet and avoid exposing sensitive data in the frontend.

narration.text: Detecting an injected provider is the first practical step of a browser dApp. The provider appears as window. ethereum when a user has a browser wallet installed. Using Web3. givenProvider is a convenient wrapper that returns the current provider when present. The common flow is: check for window. ethereum, create a new Web3 instance from it, and then request account access. A concrete code pattern from the CounterApp uses if (window. ethereum) { const web3Instance = new Web3(window. ethereum); await window. ethereum. request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' }); } which prompts the user to grant account access. A common misunderstanding is assuming detection is optional; if you skip the check, your code will fail silently in browsers without a wallet. Also remember older wallets might expose window. web3. currentProvider; for modern dApps prefer window. ethereum and Web3. givenProvider as the primary interfaces. The practical result: your app only attempts to read or send transactions after the provider is present and the user has allowed access, which keeps UX predictable and secure. Detecting the Ethereum provider means always verify window.ethereum and call eth_requestaccounts to prompt user permission before interacting with accounts or sending transactions.. In practical terms, using window.ethereum and web3.givenprovider safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Provider detection
keyIdea.text: Always verify window.ethereum and call eth_requestAccounts to prompt user permission before interacting with accounts or sending transactions.

content.html:
Definition Detecting the Ethereum provider
Quick code pattern
<!-- detection snippet --> if (window.ethereum) { const web3Instance = new Web3(window.ethereum); // ask the user to connect await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' }); } else { // fallback or show message }
This pattern ensures the wallet is present and the user explicitly approves account access before you call web3 methods that require accounts.
Tips & caution
  • Prefer window.ethereum and Web3.givenProvider for modern wallets.
  • Support a fallback message instructing users to install MetaMask if missing.
  • Avoid assuming accounts are available until eth_requestAccounts resolves.
Misconception: Detection equals permission. Detection only finds the wallet; you still must request accounts using the RPC method.

screens.title: Initializing Web3 and the Contract
screens.subtitle: A robust initWeb3 pattern for React components

narration.text: Initializing Web3 in a React component is a side effect: run it once on mount and clean up when the component unmounts. The CounterApp example defines initWeb3 that checks window. ethereum, creates a Web3 instance, requests accounts, reads accounts via web3. eth. getAccounts, and creates a new web3. eth. Contract with the contract's ABI and address. It also attaches event listeners for accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect. A practical implementation uses useCallback for stable handlers and then calls initWeb3 inside a useEffect that runs on mount. A common mistake is re-creating event listeners on every render; always add them once and remove them in the cleanup returned by useEffect to avoid duplicate subscriptions. Example pitfalls include forgetting to set loading state while initialization runs or not setting contract state before calling its methods. The outcome is a predictable initialization flow that populates web3, accounts, and contract state, ready for reads and writes. Initializing Web3 and the Contract means call initweb3 on mount, set loading and error states, instantiate web3 and contract, and register wallet event listeners with cleanup on unmount.. In practical terms, a robust initweb3 pattern for react components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Initialization pattern
keyIdea.text: Call initWeb3 on mount, set loading and error states, instantiate web3 and contract, and register wallet event listeners with cleanup on unmount.

content.html:
Process Flow Initializing Web3
Initialization steps
  1. Detect provider and create a Web3 instance.
  2. Request account access via eth_requestAccounts.
  3. Get accounts with web3.eth.getAccounts and set state.
  4. Create contract instance with new web3.eth.Contract(ABI, ADDRESS).
  5. Register accountsChanged, chainChanged, disconnect listeners and cleanup on unmount.
Example snippet
// inside initWeb3 if (window.ethereum) { const web3Instance = new Web3(window.ethereum); setWeb3(web3Instance); await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' }); const accs = await web3Instance.eth.getAccounts(); const counterContract = new web3Instance.eth.Contract(CounterABI, CONTRACT_ADDRESS); setContract(counterContract); }
Keep loading true until initialization completes and use try/catch to capture errors and set an error state for user feedback.

screens.title: State Management with React Hooks
screens.subtitle: useState and useEffect for web3, accounts, contract, and UI state

narration.text: Managing Web3-related state in React relies on a small set of hooks. useState holds the web3 instance, the connected accounts array, the contract instance, and UI primitives like loading and error. useEffect runs initialization on mount and also re-fetches data when dependencies change. For example, after initWeb3 sets web3, accounts, and contract, another useEffect watches contract and accounts to call fetchCount whenever they become available. useCallback is useful when passing handler functions to event listeners so they keep stable identity across renders. A typical pattern: initialize once, add event listeners, and remove them in the cleanup to prevent duplicated handlers. A common mistake is placing asynchronous initialization directly in the render path instead of inside useEffect, which can cause React to complain and can trigger repeated calls. Another pitfall is failing to include dependencies in dependency arrays or including changing objects that force infinite loops; prefer memoized callbacks and clear dependency lists. The goal is predictable state changes and responsive UI updates driven by wallet or contract events. State Management with React Hooks means use usestate for core objects, useeffect for side effects like initweb3 and data fetching, and usecallback for stable event handlers and functions.. In practical terms, usestate and useeffect for web3, accounts, contract, and ui state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hook patterns
keyIdea.text: Use useState for core objects, useEffect for side effects like initWeb3 and data fetching, and useCallback for stable event handlers and functions.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough State Management with Hooks
State variables
const [web3, setWeb3] = useState(null);
const [accounts, setAccounts] = useState([]);
const [contract, setContract] = useState(null);
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
const [error, setError] = useState('');
Use separate state fields so each piece can update independently and trigger minimal re-renders.
Effect to fetch data
useEffect(() => {
  if (contract && accounts.length > 0) {
    fetchCount();
  }
}, [contract, accounts, fetchCount]);
This effect ensures the UI shows the current count whenever the contract or account context becomes available or changes.

screens.title: Reading contract state (call)
screens.subtitle: Using contract.methods.<name>().call() to display data without a transaction

narration.text: Reading on-chain state from the frontend uses view or pure functions that do not require gas. In Web3. js this is done with contract. methods. someView(). call(). The Counter example uses getCount to read the current count. The fetchCount function checks for a contract instance, calls contract. methods. getCount(). call(), parses the returned value, and updates React state. This read is synchronous from the user's perspective but returns a promise and must be awaited. A common error is attempting to call view functions before the contract instance exists or before accounts are set; guard these calls with conditional checks. Another pitfall is not parsing returned values: numeric results come as strings and often require parseInt or conversion via web3. utils. The practical benefit is that read calls do not prompt the user's wallet and are safe to run frequently to refresh UI displays, though you should avoid over-polling and instead fetch on lifecycle events or after confirmed transactions. Reading contract state (call) means use call() for view functions to read contract state without gas; convert returned strings to usable numeric types before updating ui.. In practical terms, using contract.methods.<name>().call() to display data without a transaction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Read vs Write
keyIdea.text: Use call() for view functions to read contract state without gas; convert returned strings to usable numeric types before updating UI.

content.html:
Definition Reading contract state
fetchCount example
const fetchCount = useCallback(async () => {
  if (contract) {
    try {
      const currentCount = await contract.methods.getCount().call();
      setCount(parseInt(currentCount));
      setError('');
    } catch (err) {
      setError(`Error fetching count: ${err.message}`);
    }
  }
}, [contract]);
Note: parseInt is used to convert the returned string into a number for display and arithmetic in the UI.
Practical notes
  • Guard calls with if (contract) so the method exists.
  • Use try/catch to surface readable errors to the user.
  • Avoid polling too frequently; refresh after transactions or wallet events.

screens.title: Sending transactions (send)
screens.subtitle: Estimating gas and sending a state-changing transaction from the frontend

narration.text: Sending a transaction from the frontend requires the user's wallet to sign and submit it. In Web3. js you prepare a transaction with contract. methods. someStateChange(). estimateGas to estimate gas, and then call send with the from address and the gas value. The CounterApp example estimates gas for increment, then sends the transaction and awaits confirmation before re-fetching the updated count. Estimating gas provides a buffer and reduces the risk of out-of-gas reverts; the example adds 10000 units as a buffer after estimating. A typical flow is: set loading true, estimateGas, call send, await the receipt, then update UI and set loading false. Expect the MetaMask prompt and consider UX: inform users about pending confirmations and disable repeated clicks while awaiting the transaction. A common mistake is not checking for connected accounts before sending, which leads to errors. Always verify contract and accounts exist and handle failure with clear error messages. Sending transactions (send) means estimate gas before send, require a connected account, manage loading state, and re-fetch the relevant view data after confirmation.. In practical terms, estimating gas and sending a state-changing transaction from the frontend. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Transaction best practice
keyIdea.text: Estimate gas before send, require a connected account, manage loading state, and re-fetch the relevant view data after confirmation.

content.html:
Process Flow Sending transactions
incrementCount example
const incrementCount = useCallback(async () => {
  if (contract && accounts.length > 0) {
    try {
      setLoading(true);
      const gasEstimate = await contract.methods.increment().estimateGas({ from: accounts[0] });
      await contract.methods.increment().send({
        from: accounts[0],
        gas: gasEstimate + 10000
      });
      await fetchCount();
    } catch (err) {
      setError(`Error incrementing count: ${err.message}`);
    } finally {
      setLoading(false);
    }
  } else {
    setError('Web3 not initialized or no account connected.');
  }
}, [contract, accounts, fetchCount]);
UX & mistakes
  • Disable action controls while loading to prevent duplicate transactions.
  • Show a friendly confirmation message after the transaction is mined.
  • Handle user rejection of MetaMask prompts clearly rather than treating it as an unknown error.

screens.title: Handling MetaMask events
screens.subtitle: accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect — stay synchronized with the wallet

narration.text: A reliable dApp must react when the user changes accounts, switches networks, or disconnects their wallet. The provider emits events: accountsChanged when the user selects a new account, chainChanged when the network changes, and disconnect when the wallet disconnects. The CounterApp registers three handlers: handleAccountsChanged resets accounts and re-fetches data, handleChainChanged suggests a refresh and updates error state to indicate the new chain id, and handleDisconnect clears accounts and prompts the user to reconnect. A frequent mistake is to ignore these events and continue showing data for the previous account or network, which creates stale or incorrect displays. Implement handlers that either re-initialize Web3 or selectively update only the affected parts of the state. For example, if accountsChanged gives an empty array, prompt the user to connect again and clear sensitive UI data. Proper handling keeps the UI accurate and avoids confusing your users. Handling MetaMask events means subscribe to wallet events and update or clear state promptly so ui reflects the active account and network context.. In practical terms, accountschanged, chainchanged, and disconnect — stay synchronized with the wallet. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event-driven UI
keyIdea.text: Subscribe to wallet events and update or clear state promptly so UI reflects the active account and network context.

content.html:
Process Flow Handling MetaMask events
Example handlers
const handleAccountsChanged = useCallback((newAccounts) => {
  if (newAccounts.length === 0) {
    setAccounts([]); setCount(0); setError('Wallet disconnected.');
  } else if (newAccounts[0] !== accounts[0]) {
    setAccounts(newAccounts);
    if (contract) fetchCount();
  }
}, [accounts, contract]);

const handleChainChanged = useCallback((chainId) => {
  setError(`Network changed to Chain ID: ${parseInt(chainId)}. Please refresh if issues persist.`);
}, []);

const handleDisconnect = useCallback((error) => {
  setError('MetaMask disconnected. Please reconnect.');
  setAccounts([]); setCount(0);
}, []);
Best practices
  • Register listeners once during init and remove them in cleanup to avoid duplicates.
  • On chainChanged consider re-initializing web3 or prompting the user to refresh.
  • Clear data that depends on the account when the wallet disconnects to avoid leaks.

screens.title: Loading & Error States
screens.subtitle: Presenting clear UX while asynchronous Web3 calls run or fail

narration.text: Asynchronous operations are central to dApp UX: provider detection, account requests, contract calls, and sending transactions all return promises. Design your UI to communicate these states: a loading indicator when initialization or a transaction is pending, success confirmations after operations complete, and clear error messages when something fails. In the CounterApp pattern, the loading boolean covers initial Web3 setup and transaction operations; specific error strings hold user-facing messages. For example, if fetchCount fails, set an error like 'Error fetching count:...' and leave the previous count visible only if it's still valid. A common mistake is showing raw error objects or stack traces to users; instead, parse the message and provide actionable guidance like 'Please connect your wallet' or 'Transaction rejected'. Another valuable UX pattern is optimistic UI: disable the increment button while waiting for confirmation to prevent duplicate submissions. Clear loading and error handling prevents confusion and leads to a smoother dApp experience. Loading & Error States means use loading flags and user-friendly error messages to keep the ui predictable during provider initialization and transaction lifecycles.. In practical terms, presenting clear ux while asynchronous web3 calls run or fail. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UX for async
keyIdea.text: Use loading flags and user-friendly error messages to keep the UI predictable during provider initialization and transaction lifecycles.

content.html:
Comparison Loading vs Error UX
Loading state
Use a single loading flag for initialization and separate flags for transactions. Show spinners and disable action controls during pending operations to avoid duplicates.
Example: setLoading(true) before estimateGas and send; setLoading(false) in finally to re-enable the UI.
Error handling
  • Show clear, actionable messages rather than raw error objects.
  • If wallet not detected, instruct to install MetaMask.
  • If network mismatch, suggest switching networks or refreshing.
Misconception: Hiding errors improves UX. In reality, actionable errors prevent user confusion and reduce support requests.

screens.title: Gas estimation and frontend safety
screens.subtitle: Why estimateGas matters and how to avoid common pitfalls

narration.text: Estimating gas from the frontend gives you a clearer idea of how much gas a transaction will consume and helps prevent out-of-gas failures that would waste user time and funds. The CounterApp uses contract. methods. increment(). estimateGas({ from: accounts[0] }) before calling send. Adding a modest buffer to the estimate accounts for small state changes that might affect gas cost between estimation and submission. However, remember that estimateGas itself is a simulation and can fail for different reasons, so wrap it in try/catch and present helpful messages if estimation fails. Another frontend safety note is never to hardcode private keys or place signing logic in client code; always rely on the injected wallet for signing. Use environment variables for contract addresses and network configuration so production builds are configurable. A common misconception is believing that gas estimation guarantees success; it reduces risk but you should still handle failed transactions gracefully and show feedback to the user. Gas estimation and frontend safety means estimate gas before sending, add a safe buffer, catch estimation errors, and never move signing out of the user's wallet.. In practical terms, why estimategas matters and how to avoid common pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Gas safety
keyIdea.text: Estimate gas before sending, add a safe buffer, catch estimation errors, and never move signing out of the user's wallet.

content.html:
Definition Gas estimation and safety
Estimation example
const gasEstimate = await contract.methods.increment().estimateGas({ from: accounts[0] });
await contract.methods.increment().send({ from: accounts[0], gas: gasEstimate + 10000 });
Add a buffer to the estimate and present clear errors if estimation fails.
Practical tips
  • Catch estimation errors and show guidance rather than raw exceptions.
  • Don't expose private keys; rely on MetaMask for signing.
  • Keep addresses and network configs in environment variables for production.

screens.title: Build the Counter DApp (lab walkthrough)
screens.subtitle: Scaffold a React project, install Web3, and wire the CounterApp component

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks through building the Counter DApp from scratch. Start by creating a new React project using a fast template, install web3, and place your CounterABI. json inside src. Replace the starter App with the CounterApp component and update CONTRACT_ADDRESS to your deployed Counter contract on Ganache. Run Ganache and import one of its accounts into MetaMask, connecting MetaMask to your local RPC so the wallet can sign transactions. Start the dev server and open the app; you should be prompted by MetaMask to connect when initWeb3 runs. Once connected, the app will call getCount and show the current value. Click the increment control to trigger the transaction, confirm it in MetaMask, and observe the count update after the transaction is mined. A common mistake is forgetting to switch MetaMask to the Ganache network or failing to import the Ganache private key; both prevent transactions. This lab reinforces the earlier patterns and gives hands-on experience with provider detection, contract instantiation, data fetching, gas estimation, and event handling. Build the Counter DApp (lab walkthrough) means a working local counter dapp that connects to metamask and ganache, reads the count, and sends increments while handling wallet events.. In practical terms, scaffold a react project, install web3, and wire the counterapp component. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: A working local Counter DApp that connects to MetaMask and Ganache, reads the count, and sends increments while handling wallet events.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity Build the Counter DApp
Step-by-step
1. Scaffold
Create a React project with your preferred tool and install web3.
2. Add ABI
Copy CounterABI.json to src and set CONTRACT_ADDRESS to your deployed contract.
3. Wire CounterApp
Paste the CounterApp component, initialize web3 on mount, and fetch the count.
4. Connect MetaMask
Start Ganache, import a private key to MetaMask, and switch MetaMask to the local RPC.
Run & verify
  1. npm run dev and open the app URL.
  2. Approve account access in MetaMask when prompted.
  3. Observe the initial count and confirm increment transactions in MetaMask.
  4. If something is wrong, check network configuration and the contract address environment variable.

narration.text: These core concepts are the practical vocabulary of React dApp development. window. ethereum is the injected provider from browser wallets and is your gateway to the user's account and network. eth_requestAccounts is the RPC method that asks the user to approve account access; detection alone is not permission. narration.text: Keep these three reminders handy as you implement the CounterApp or any frontend dApp. First, always check for a provider and then request account access; detection without permission doesn't let you sign transactions. Second, treat read calls with call() as safe and inexpensive but always convert returned strings to the appropriate numeric types before displaying or computing. Third, listen for wallet events like accountsChanged and chainChanged so your UI can refresh or clear sensitive data when the user changes account or network. Together these reminders reduce errors, improve security, and make your dApp feel responsive. When in doubt, surface clear guidance to the user: ask them to connect, switch networks, or retry a failed transaction with actionable steps.
